newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: FORECAST-Czech March trade gap seen 17 bln crowns.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST-Czech March trade gap seen 17 bln crowns.

text.p: The Czech trade deficit is expected to grow faster in March, with the monthly increase seen at about 17 billion crowns up from 13.7 billion in February, a Reuters poll of economists showed on Monday.
March trade figures are to be released by the Czech Statistical Bureau (CSU) at 9 a.m. (0700 GMT) on Tuesday.
Most economists surveyed said they expect the widening trend of the trade deficit seen over the past few months to continue, especially when seasonal adjustments are factored into the equation.
"I don't think it will be an excellent figure, but considerably worse than in February though still not a disaster," said Martin Kupka, an economist at Patria Finance.

"I think there is some seasonality also involved. Last year, the figure was relatively steady in January and February, and then in March there was a jump up. We have seen the same so far this year," Kupka added.
The January and February 1997 monthly trade gaps were both between 13 and 14 billion crowns, putting the total deficit at 27.2 billion crowns for the first two months of the year.
The monthly deficit in both January and February 1996 was roughly eight billion crowns, and then jumped in March by some 11 billion crowns to a first quarter gap of 27.1 billion.
Analysts say the trade balance has been hurt by a downturn in western European economies. The effects of a recovery in demand have yet to make an impact on Czech exports.

They added that the March shortfall would also be exacerbated by importers rushing to stock up on goods knowing the government was planning to announce import restriction measures in April, and possibly a devaluation of the crown.
"The expectations that the crown would be depreciated (either officially or by the market) probably has played a role with decisions of importers," one analyst surveyed said.
The widening trade deficit -- which has consistently shown the rate of import growth exceeding export growth -- has become one of a number of growing problems for the Czech economy.

On April 16 the government announced sweeping pro-growth measures aimed at reducing growing budget and trade deficits, while spurring growth, dampening demand for imports and adding confidence to beleaguered capital markets.
But the moves did not include any change to monetary or exchange rate policies.

The foreign exchange and money markets are expected to show little reaction to the figures -- as the worsening Czech trade balance has been long built into crown rates -- as long as the results do not vary greatly from the estimates.
The crown was trading at 1.75 percent below its dollar/mark basket midpoint, after opening at about -0.60 percent.
"Foreign investors are closing their positions, it's been continuing since Friday evening," Breta Tichanek, a dealer at ING Bank told Reuters.
"It is partially due to tomorrow's trade balance figures, and partially a fear of possible interest rate changes this week," he added.
